scenes.heading: Planning a practical investigation
scenes.sub: A good experiment starts with a good plan
scenes.say: A good investigation doesn't start in the lab. It starts with a careful plan, so your experiment tests the right question, gives results you can trust, and is safe.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Testing if more sugar makes cookies spread
scenes.science: Change one variable, measure one, keep the rest the same
scenes.breaks: at home you might judge cookies by eye, but in chemistry you must measure quantitatively with suitable equipment.
scenes.say: Say you want to know if more sugar makes cookies spread. Sugar is the independent variable, the thing you change. How wide the cookies spread is the dependent variable, what you measure. Oven temperature and baking time are controlled variables. Change those too, and you can't tell what caused the spreading.

scenes.heading: Know your variables

right.title: Dependent
points: e.g. volume of H₂ in 60 s

scenes.say: Remember: I change, D detects. The independent variable is the one you change, like acid concentration. The dependent variable is the data you collect, like the volume of hydrogen. Everything else stays controlled: one dial at a time.

scenes.heading: Writing a hypothesis
points: Data support or refute; never prove
scenes.say: A hypothesis follows a pattern: if this changes, then that will increase or decrease, because of a scientific reason. Don't forget the direction or the because. And results can only support or refute a hypothesis. They never prove it.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: How does temperature (20–60 °C) affect the time for 2 cm of Mg ribbon to dissolve in 50 mL of 1.0 mol L⁻¹ HCl?
lines: DV: time for Mg to dissolve (s)
Controlled: Mg length, acid volume, conc.
scenes.say: A student tests how temperature affects the time magnesium takes to dissolve in acid. Temperature is the independent variable; time is the dependent variable. Magnesium length and acid volume and concentration are controlled. Hypothesis: higher temperature, less time, because particles collide more often and with more energy.

scenes.heading: Don't mix these up
scenes.say: A control is a baseline set-up you compare against. Controlled variables are the factors you keep constant, and you should say how, like using a water bath at twenty-five degrees.
scenes.caption: A control is a baseline set-up you compare against. Controlled variables are the factors you keep constant, and you should say how, like using a water bath at 25 °C.

scenes.heading: Method self-check
steps: At least 5 values of the IV
Each hazard has a control measure
scenes.say: Check your method. Do at least three repeats, test at least five values, and write numbered steps someone else could follow. Every hazard in your risk assessment needs a matching control measure, so check the safety data sheet.

points: Change one IV; measure one DV
scenes.say: Quick recap. Change one independent variable and measure one dependent variable. Keep everything else controlled. Write your hypothesis as if, then, because. And plan for repeats, safety and ethics. Now try the practice questions!
